    Orchestrating Claude: what we built, checked and decided

    A 17-lesson teaching page and an agent harness playbook, with the research behind them, three expert reviews, a 13-part rework, four more independent reviews, and the checks that gate every change. One file, offline, searchable.

    01

    About this compendium

    What is here and how to use it offline.

    This file collects everything from one working session on 24 October 2026. The session built and reviewed Orchestrating Claude, a 17-lesson teaching page about goals, checks, helper agents and unattended runs, and the Agent Harness Playbook that the page summarises. It includes the research, every review, every decision, the issue that drove the rework, and the scripts that check and rebuild the work.

    It is one HTML file with no network requests, so it reads offline. Press / to search: results come from every section, including the full text of the page and the playbook. The page itself is embedded in the Teaching page section, and the live version is at claude.ai (private to its owner until shared).

    Start here (ENTRY.md)

    The entry point for a session in another project: the scenario router and the phase table.

    Source: ENTRY.md

    Read this first when another project calls this guide, through /guide, a CLAUDE.md pointer or a pasted prompt. It routes your request to a few playbook sections, at most one runbook and one template. Never load the whole playbook: it is about 1,500 lines.

    How to use it

    1. Two folders. GUIDE is the folder that holds this file: its full path in a clone, or, with no clone, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/seintun/claude-guides/main (https://seintun.github.io/claude-guides also serves main). If your link is a fork or names a branch, use https://raw.githubusercontent.com/<owner>/<repo>/<branch> from it. Every path in this file, runbook links included, is relative to GUIDE. Your project is your current directory. The guide gives advice; your project gets the work.
    2. Find your row in the scenario router. If none fits, use the phase table.
    3. Load only the row's sections: python3 -I GUIDE/tools/section.py 9.5 F prints §9.5 and Template F, and nothing else. Ids: 9.5 or 17A for a section, F for a template, law-7 for a law, cs:3 for the cheat sheet. --list lists every id. Template letters are ids too: add them to the same call when you need the artifact the row's output names. No clone? Fetch the row's bundle from GUIDE/routes/: the row's sections and templates in one file, such as GUIDE/routes/row-7.md for row 7 or GUIDE/routes/phase-3.md for phase 3. The bundle already holds the row's templates. For a single id, fetch GUIDE/sections/<id>.md (cs:3 is sections/cs-3.md). Fetch raw text: a summarising fetch tool can shorten a file. GUIDE/guide-index.json holds this router as JSON.
    4. Open the runbook (GUIDE/wiki/<name>.md, about 80 lines) only if you need its steps and checklist.
    5. Produce the row's output in your project, and follow the rules at the end.

    Rows marked thin have no full recipe in the playbook. They route to the nearest sections and name the gap; say so to the user instead of filling it from memory. Grades in the sections: (P) primary, (S) second-hand, (R) research, (D) design advice. "Page Lesson N" in a runbook means a lesson of the teaching page, GUIDE/site/index.html.

    Rules that apply everywhere

    • Goal first. One sentence of result, 2 to 5 Done-when checks a command or a person can run, a budget and a stop-and-ask list. Load B.
    • One writer. One agent edits a set of files. Helpers read, search and review, and return findings with paths. Load 7.
    • Fresh review. A reviewer gets the work and the criteria, never your conclusion. Load law-7.
    • Receipts. Mark every check PASS, FAIL or NOT RUN, with its command. NOT RUN is not PASS. Load 9.4.
    • Two strikes. If the same check fails twice for the same reason, stop and ask for a second opinion. Load B.
    • Reviews end. Only a blocker with evidence reopens a review, a re-review reads the fix for open and new blockers, only the reviewer or a human closes a blocker unfixed, and after two rounds a human decides. Load 9.2.
    • Code over words. Anything that must never happen gets a deny rule, a hook or a gate, not only a sentence. Load law-9.
    • Records on disk. Decisions go to the project's docs/ and are committed; scratch stays out of git. Open GUIDE/wiki/records.md.
    • Loops are bounded. Every loop needs a stop condition, a retry cap and a cost ceiling. Load 11.3.

    Orchestration index

    The phase index: eight phases, what to read in each, and review checklists.

    Source: orchestration-index.md

    This is an agent-readable entry point. The agent reads this file first, then pulls only the playbook sections a phase names.

    Sources:

    • playbook/agent-harness-playbook.md is the guiding star. The § numbers below refer to it.
    • playbook/claude-cheat-sheet.md covers commands, a prompt template and signs that a run is stuck.
    • wiki/ holds step-by-step runbooks for each phase.

    How an agent uses this file

    1. Find the current phase in the table below.
    2. Read only the sections listed for that phase. Do not load the whole playbook.
    3. Run the phase's review checklist against the work, citing the section for every finding.
    4. Report each item as PASS, FAIL or NOT RUN with evidence (file, line or command). Never mark PASS without evidence.

    Reusable review prompt:

    Read orchestration-index.md. We are in phase <N>. Pull only the sections it lists for
that phase, then review <file or plan or diff> against that phase's checklist.
For each item, return PASS / FAIL / NOT RUN, the evidence, and the playbook section.
Finish with up to three fixes that block, or say that none do. Do not edit anything.

    Review checklists

    1. Shape

    • The problem is stated as user pain, not as a solution.
    • Grilling ran one question at a time and stopped once the answers converged (§5.2).
    • Out-of-scope items are written down.

    2. Brief

    • The goal is one sentence and is an outcome, not a list of steps (Law 3).
    • "Done when" is checkable by a command or an explicit acceptance list.
    • Constraints name what must not change.
    • "Stop and ask if" lists the risky and ambiguous cases.
    • A budget is set: time, tokens or attempts.

    3. Plan

    • Slices are vertical, and each one is testable on its own.
    • Each hard-to-reverse decision is recorded with the reason for it.
    • Open questions are listed and not silently assumed.
    • Risky plans had a fresh-context critic (Law 7).
    • Unfamiliar work searched the repo first, then the official docs, then other projects for ideas, and every new dependency was vetted (§5.4).

    4. Orchestrate

    • There is one writer per set of files; helpers only read or review (§6).
    • Each subagent brief has a goal, scope, what is already ruled out and the return format (§7, §16C).
    • Fan-out is justified by independence, not by parallelism alone.
    • Model per role: cheap scouts, a strong architect and reviewer.

    5. Build

    • Context stays lean: /compact at phase boundaries, files rather than chat for state (§8).
    • The same failure twice triggers a stop and ranked hypotheses, not a third blind retry.
    • Progress is committed in small steps.

    6. Check

    • Every acceptance criterion maps to a gate (§9.1).
    • Receipts use the §9.4 format, with commands.
    • The checker is not the maker (Law 7).
    • Tests were not weakened or deleted to pass.
    • One acceptance check sat outside the builder's reach, run by CI or the Stop gate (§9.3).
    • Hooks enforce what words only request (Law 9, §9.5).

    7. Overnight

    • A state file and a progress log exist so a fresh context can resume (§11.1, §16E).
    • The loop has a stop condition, a budget cap and an attempt cap (§11.3).
    • Permissions are pre-approved for safe actions only; nothing irreversible runs unattended (§10).
    • It works on a branch or worktree, never on main.
    • The morning report lists what passed, what failed and what is waiting on you.

    8. Learn

    • Each repeated correction became a rule; dead rules were pruned (Law 8).
    • Failures became eval tasks (§13, §16J).
    • A mined rule or skill stayed only if re-running the evals showed it helps (§13).
    • A retro was written (§16I).

    Start a task

    Source: wiki/start-a-task.md

    Use this page when you have a pain point or an idea and need a goal Claude can check and an issue an agent can finish.

    Steps

    1. Frame the outcome. Name who struggles, what progress they want and the metric to move. Do not go on until the outcome has a number. §5.1 (D)
    2. Map the assumptions. Rank the desirability, viability and feasibility assumptions by importance and evidence, and test the important, unproven ones first (P). Let the agent draft the feasibility items from the code (D).
    3. Grill anything above trivial. Skip it for a one-line fix (D). Run Template K: one question per message with a recommended answer and its cost, no question the agent can answer from the code, a decision log in the repo, and a stop when no branch is open or the question cap is hit (D). §5.2
    4. Shape a pitch and fix the appetite. A pitch has a problem, an appetite, a solution, rabbit holes and no-gos. Appetite is a time budget, not an estimate, and the no-gos become the agent's scope fence (P). Park pitches you do not bet on instead of keeping a backlog (P).
    5. Pick the spec weight by risk and novelty. A small fix needs an issue with a check. A normal feature needs a grill log, a one-page spec with Given/When/Then scenarios and open questions, and sliced issues. A large or risky change adds a research doc, an architecture decision record, the critic and human sign-off (D). §5.3
    6. Write the spec in a fresh session from the decision log. Make every criterion observable and write the failure cases into the spec, since requirements usually go missing there (P). List undecided policy under Open Questions, because LLM-drafted PRDs state unagreed policy as fact (S).
    7. Slice into agent-ready issues with Template L. Each issue states an outcome, a check, a boundary, dependencies, open questions and a risk. Build a thin end-to-end slice first, split vertically through the layers, and keep throwaway spikes out of production issues (P).
    8. Size and risk-rate each issue. Treat a few person-days of human work as the ceiling for one issue and prefer smaller (D). Set Risk by a rule (paths touched, new dependencies, schema or auth changes), and when the rule and a person disagree, take the higher (D).
    9. Turn each issue into a goal with Template B. Write the result in one sentence, then list two to five Done-when checks that a command or a person can run, the constraints, a budget and a stop-and-ask list, as page Lesson 4 (Goals) shows. Ask for a receipt: each line marked PASS, FAIL or NOT RUN, with its command.
    10. Run a QA loop. An upfront spec never catches everything, so turn each QA finding into a new issue and send it back to slicing (P).

    Checklist

    • [ ] The outcome has a number and names the person who struggles.
    • [ ] Every important, unproven assumption has a test or a spike.
    • [ ] The grill log lives in the repo, and I confirmed its summary.
    • [ ] The appetite and the no-gos are written down.
    • [ ] The spec weight matches the risk and novelty of the change.
    • [ ] Every issue has a runnable check, a named boundary and a Risk set by a rule.
    • [ ] Open questions are listed, not guessed.
    • [ ] The goal has Done-when lines that a command or a person can check, and a stop-and-ask list.

    Templates

    • Template K. Grill prompt: shared understanding before any plan or spec.
    • Template L. Agent-ready issue: the issue an agent can finish.
    • Template B. Task contract (goal prompt): the goal, with done-when, budget and stop rules.

    Watch out for

    • Goals with no "done when". Claude guesses and polishes what you did not ask for, as page Lesson 4 (Goals) shows (§15).
    • Acting on wrong assumptions. The model proceeds without checking (S). Counter it with a discovery interview up front, "state your assumptions" in the plan, and plan approval (§14).
    • Not asking when confused. The model often keeps going (S). Add an explicit stop-and-ask list and a confidence field in receipts.
    • Upfront specs that miss edge cases. Matt Pocock says QA keeps surfacing them (P). Keep a QA loop whose findings become new issues.
    • One-line tickets. They drop edge cases, and a PRD that says what and why still lacks the exact change, boundary and check an agent needs (S).
    • Rounds of questions. Rounds are faster but get skimmed (D), so ask one question at a time.

    Grill before you plan

    Source: wiki/grill.md

    Use this page when a request is bigger than a one-line fix and you and the agent don't yet share the design. The grill runs before any plan, spec or code. The /grill skill in skills/grill packages these rules. It runs only when you type /grill, never on its own.

    Steps

    1. Decide whether to grill. Grill anything above trivial, and skip it for a one-line fix (D). §5.2
    2. Look before you ask. The agent reads the code, docs and data first, and never asks you a fact it can find; it reports what it found instead (D). For a wide sweep it sends read-only helpers in parallel, so the questions start from facts. §5.2
    3. Ask one question per message, with the agent's recommended answer and what it costs. Rounds are faster but get skimmed (D). §5.2
    4. Give every question the same shape (D):
      • 2 to 4 options, with the recommendation first, marked "(Recommended)";
      • each option says what it implies and what it costs;
      • the question text says why the recommendation wins;
      • split a question that needs more than 4 options.

    In Claude Code, ask with the AskUserQuestion tool, one question per call, so the user picks instead of typing. Where the tool is missing, ask in plain text with lettered options.

    1. Walk the design tree. Settle prerequisite questions before the ones that depend on them, and cover who struggles and when, the outcome metric, the appetite, no-gos, rabbit holes, failure cases and open questions. Template K
    2. Log each decision in the repo as you go, not only in chat: date, question, answer, reason (D). See records. Use docs/discovery/<topic>.md, or the Decisions list of the plan file when one exists.
    3. Stop when no branch is open or the question cap is hit, then summarize the decisions for the user to confirm (D). §5.2
    4. Keep approval out of the grill. A go-ahead to build, commit or publish waits for the user's explicit yes, not a picked option (D).
    5. Write the spec or plan in a fresh session from the decision log, so the interview's clutter stays out of the build (D). §5.2

    Checklist: validate a grill

    Per question:

    • [ ] It could not be answered from the code, docs or data.
    • [ ] It is the only question in the message.
    • [ ] It has 2 to 4 options, the recommended one first and marked.
    • [ ] Each option names what it implies and what it costs, and the question says why the recommendation wins.

    Per session:

    • [ ] Facts were looked up before the first question.
    • [ ] Every answer is in the decision log with its reason.
    • [ ] The grill stopped at the cap or with no branch open, and the user confirmed the summary.
    • [ ] No plan, spec or code was written during the grill.

    Templates

    • Template K. Grill prompt: the paste-in version of these rules.
    • Template B. Task contract (goal prompt): what the grill's decisions turn into.
    • Template D. Plan file: its Decisions list can hold the grill log.

    Test the skill

    skills/grill/test.sh runs one fresh claude -p session in a throwaway project outside the repository. It asks for a grill on "add full-text search to our notes service". The project's README answers two questions the grill must not ask: the database (PostgreSQL) and the test command. check_transcript.py then checks the session's first message against 8 rules:

    CheckRule
    grill-1It looked at the project before asking
    grill-2It reported a fact it found (PostgreSQL) instead of asking for it
    grill-3It asked no question the README answers
    grill-4One question in the message
    grill-52 to 4 options
    grill-6The recommended option comes first, and only one is recommended
    grill-7It wrote no plan, spec or code
    grill-8The session ended without an error

    Last result, 2026-10-24: all 8 checks passed in 3 of 3 runs (Sonnet, through claude -p). The first run failed grill-5 and grill-6 because the checker missed the model's option format, so the checker now accepts the common ones and prints the message when a check fails.

    Limits: the test checks the first message only, with one fixture and one model. Model output varies, so run it 3 times before trusting a change to the skill (§9.3 on pass^k). The --installed flag tests the /grill command itself, once you have linked it.

    Worked example

    The plan for this guide's entry point began with a 3-question grill. The decisions are in docs/plans/guide-entry.md.

    • Facts first. Before the first question, three helpers in parallel audited the entry files, mapped 18 scenarios to playbook coverage, and checked how skills and CLAUDE.md imports load. None of those findings became a question.
    • Three questions, one per message, each with the recommendation first: how far "callable from anywhere" should reach, how to install the skill, and how to route scenarios the playbook covers only partly. The third was asked only after the coverage audit found 7 partial scenarios.
    • Approval stayed separate. The plan was approved after the grill, as its own step.

    Watch out for

    • Rounds of questions. They are faster but get skimmed (D). Keep to one per message.
    • Asking for facts. Every question the agent could have answered itself spends your attention.
    • A picked option taken as approval. An option chooses between designs; it doesn't authorize work.
    • Versions of Pocock's grill-me skill differ on pacing. One asks one question at a time, while the current one asks in rounds (P). §5.2

    Orchestrate

    Source: wiki/orchestrate.md

    Use this page when a task is big enough that you must decide whether the lead agent should hand part of it to helper agents.

    Steps

    1. Default to one writer. One agent writes each set of files, and each builder works in its own git worktree (D). The evidence backs this: pick the topology by task shape and default to one writer (R). §19.1
    2. Ask whether you need a helper at all. Start with the simplest solution, because many tasks need one well-built call, not an agent (P). If one call with good context is enough, stop here.
    3. Send a helper when the job fits. Send wide reading where you only need the conclusion, jobs that do not depend on each other, judgments from someone who did not do the work, and cheap search or summary jobs. Keep a job in the lead when it is a handful of steps, needs every detail, takes longer to brief than to do, or would have two helpers editing the same files. Both lists come from page Lesson 6 (Orchestration).
    4. Match the task shape to a pattern. Known steps and independent parts: parallel sectioning. Known steps that depend on each other: a prompt chain with checks. Unknown steps and read-heavy work: orchestrator-workers. Work that spans many sessions: an initializer plus incremental workers, or a Ralph loop. Anything else: one agent running plan → critique → build. For one trustworthy metric use a hill-climbing loop; for a judgment call with no test use a council or an adversarial review. §6
    5. Write the brief. Give each helper an objective, context (what is already ruled out), scope, tools, output, budget and a stop rule (D). Vague briefs cause duplicated work and gaps (P). Use Template C for read-only work.
    6. Say what comes back. Ask for a short summary, findings with file:line or URL and a confidence, unknowns and artifact paths (D). Have helpers write long output to files and pass paths back, to avoid a "game of telephone" (P). For unfamiliar work, search the repo first, then the official docs, then other projects for ideas, not code (D). §5.4
    7. Scale effort to the task. Use 1 agent and 3 to 10 tool calls for simple fact-finding, 2 to 4 subagents with 10 to 15 calls each for a direct comparison, and more than 10 only for complex research (P). Cap agents per task and calls per agent in the lead's prompt (D).
    8. Launch in parallel and keep the plan on disk. Anthropic reports that spawning subagents in parallel cut research time by up to 90% (P). The lead saves its plan, because context beyond 200,000 tokens gets truncated (P); Template D is a plan file.
    9. Treat each report as a claim. The lead re-checks any claim that drives a decision, and passes summaries and file paths between agents, never raw transcripts (D).
    10. Stop on a repeat failure. If the same check fails twice for the same reason, stop and get a second opinion from a fresh agent instead of retrying (D). §4

    Checklist

    • [ ] One agent writes each set of files, and each builder has its own worktree.
    • [ ] I can say why this task needs helpers, or I kept it in the lead.
    • [ ] I named the task shape and the pattern that fits it.
    • [ ] Every helper has a written brief with objective, scope, output, budget and stop rule.
    • [ ] Helpers return summaries and file paths, not transcripts.
    • [ ] The fan-out has a cap on agents per task and calls per agent.
    • [ ] The lead re-checked every claim that drives a decision.
    • [ ] The plan file is current.

    Templates

    • Template C. Subagent brief: read-only work for a helper. For a builder, use the brief schema in §7 and set the scope to what it may touch.
    • Template D. Plan file: slices, each with its test and rollback.
    • Template B. Task contract (goal prompt): sets the helper budget and the second-opinion rule.

    Watch out for

    • Fanning out tightly coupled edits. In Google Research's study, multi-agent setups lost 39 to 70% on sequential planning (R). Coupled edits belong in one agent (§15).
    • Agents with no central lead. Independent agents amplified errors 17.2× versus 4.4× with a central orchestrator, both relative to a single agent (R).
    • Adding agents to a task one agent already handles. Gains shrank, and often turned negative, once a single agent scored above about 45%; that is a fitted estimate, not a hard cutoff (R).
    • Ignoring the token bill. Orchestrator-workers costs about 15 times the tokens of a chat, where a single agent uses about 4 times (P).
    • Agent teams. They are experimental, off by default and have no worktree isolation, so partition the files yourself (P).
    • Passing transcripts between agents. Pass files and summaries instead (§15).

    Verify

    Source: wiki/verify.md

    Use this page when you need to make "done" provable: what to check, who checks it, and what proof the agent hands back.

    Steps

    1. Write each criterion as a scenario. "Export matches the screen" becomes "Given 3 rows filtered to 2, the CSV has 2 rows." Write Given/When/Then declaratively, in 3 to 5 steps (P). §9.1
    2. Turn the scenario into an automated check, then a gate. The path is criterion → scenario → automated check → gate → receipt. For example, a test in npm test, enforced by a Stop hook and a CI required check (D).
    3. Require a receipt. For each criterion, record PASS, FAIL or NOT RUN with the command and its output, then list what is not done and the next step. NOT RUN is not PASS (D). §9.4
    4. Pick a rung on the trust ladder by risk. Rung 1, "the agent says it's done", is never enough. Rung 2 shows the command and output, rung 3 has a hook rerun the checks, rung 4 adds a fresh reviewer, rung 5 an adversary, and rung 6 a human (D). §9.2
    5. Install the Stop hook (Template F). Exit code 2 blocks the stop and feeds stderr back to Claude, and stop_hook_active tells the hook Claude is already continuing (P). Make the script executable, force one failing test and confirm the hook returns exit 2 (D).
    6. Add the formatter hook (Template G). It runs after Edit or Write, uses the project's own Prettier and leaves gate and config files alone (D). A PostToolUse exit code 2 shows stderr, but the tool has already run (P).
    7. Make tests immutable to the builder. Back the rule with a hook or CODEOWNERS on test paths, and have the reviewer inspect every test diff, including mocks that replace the behaviour under test (D). Anthropic's long-running harness called removing or editing tests unacceptable (P). Keep one acceptance check outside the builder's workspace, run by CI or the Stop gate (D). §9.3
    8. Check in order, cheapest first. Use rules-based feedback (lint, types, tests), then visual feedback through a browser for UI, then an LLM judge (P). Give any judge a rubric (P), use one from a different model family than the work and repeat it (D), and never make it the only gate (D). §9.3
    9. Get an independent review. The maker is not the checker. A fresh reviewer gets the artifact and the criteria, never the author's reasoning or conclusion, and sources are anonymized when it compares candidates (D). Keep the fresh-eyes review even when tests are green (S). Bound it: only a blocker with evidence reopens a review, a re-review reads the fix diff for open and new blockers, only the reviewer or a human closes a blocker without a fix, and after two rounds a human decides (D). §9.2; evidence in research/bounded-review-evidence.md.
    10. Measure repeated runs for unattended work. Track pass^k (all k runs succeed), not only pass@k. At 75% per-run success, three runs in a row all succeed only about 42% of the time (P). Decide on purpose which tiers get line-by-line human review (D).

    Checklist

    • [ ] Every criterion has a scenario and a command that checks it.
    • [ ] The Stop hook is executable, and I forced a failing test to confirm exit 2.
    • [ ] The receipt lists PASS, FAIL or NOT RUN per criterion, with the command.
    • [ ] NOT RUN is not counted as PASS.
    • [ ] Test paths are protected from the builder by a hook or CODEOWNERS.
    • [ ] A reviewer with a fresh context got the diff and the criteria only.
    • [ ] No LLM judge is the only gate.
    • [ ] I chose which risk tiers get line-by-line human review.

    Templates

    • Template F. Stop hook that blocks "done" while tests fail: retries up to a cap, then logs the give-up.
    • Template G. PostToolUse formatter: formats each edited file with the project's own Prettier.
    • Template B. Task contract (goal prompt): the Done-when lines and "NOT RUN is not PASS".
    • Template A. CLAUDE.md skeleton: its Never list holds the receipt rule and the test rule.

    Watch out for

    • The builder grading its own work. Also a reviewer that read the author's conclusion first (§15). Hand over code and criteria only.
    • Edited tests and early victory. Models edit, disable or delete tests to make them pass, and declare victory early (P). Counter with a test-immutability rule, a JSON feature list, end-to-end tests and a Stop hook (§14).
    • A gate that silently turns off. A non-executable hook script exits 126, which Claude Code treats as a non-blocking error (D). Stop does not run on a user interrupt, and API errors fire StopFailure instead (P). --bare skips your hooks, so run the gate as a CI step (D).
    • Green tests, broken spec. One practitioner's Ralph run passed 28 tests and then failed a fresh review on a real spec breach (S).
    • An LLM judge as the only gate. The Agent SDK guidance calls it not very robust on its own (P).
    • Normalization of deviance. Simon Willison wrote that he no longer reviews every line of agent output and named this risk himself (P). A near-100% approval rate with falling review time is the warning sign (D).

    Run unattended

    Source: wiki/run-unattended.md

    Use this page before Claude runs a loop, a schedule or a cloud session while you are not watching.

    Steps

    1. Check that the work suits an unattended run. Good fits are a well-specified backlog with strong tests (a Ralph loop, or day shift and night shift) and one trustworthy metric (a hill-climbing loop). A loop burns tokens and drifts if the specs or tests are weak (D). §6
    2. Pick the surface. /loop runs in your session, at a 1-minute minimum or self-paced; it expires after 7 days, skips missed runs and dies with the session (P). Cloud scheduled tasks (/schedule) have a 1-hour minimum for timed triggers, start from a fresh clone and push to a claude/ branch (P). Desktop tasks need the app open and the machine awake (P).
    3. Copy a Template H prompt. Fill in what to watch, the one small action allowed, the end condition and the forbidden actions. Make the action safe to run twice, and ask for one status line per run, with "no change" when nothing changed (D).
    4. Write the stop condition and the retry cap. Stop when every check passes, or after N iterations, minutes or dollars, and stop after two failures with the same cause (D). Do not lean on the Stop-hook continuation cap of 8, because it is a backstop (P).
    5. Set a cost ceiling. Use --max-budget-usd on headless runs and cap the fan-out in the lead's prompt (P, D). Read cost from OpenTelemetry or the Console, not the local /usage estimate (P).
    6. Give the results a home outside the chat. Use a file, a ticket or a PR comment (D). Cloud runs start from a fresh clone, so keep loop state in a ticket, a PR comment or a named branch (P). For work that spans sessions, use an initializer session, a JSON feature list that starts at passes: false and a progress file (P), and let a verifier or the gate flip passes (D).
    7. Hook the events. Add a StopFailure hook that writes a marker and notifies you, because API errors and rate limits skip the Stop gate (P, D). Hang phone pings or approval routing on Notification, Stop and PermissionRequest, and set telemetry variables on cloud environments too (P).
    8. Write the kill switch before the first run. One page: disable the scheduled task or workflow, stop or archive the session, revoke the tokens it used and revert its branch (D). §18
    9. Sandbox the run and strip secrets. Use a dev container or Docker locally, keep the network level minimal and keep production keys out of cloud environments (D). For claude -p in CI, use --bare or a trusted checkout, and run your gate as a CI step (P, D).
    10. Judge the first run by what it leaves behind. An overnight run should leave a clean state and an accurate receipt; that is the roadmap's condition for moving up from Level 4 (D). Check for paused runs, not only failed ones, because a cloud scheduled task can stop and wait for an answer (P).

    Checklist

    • [ ] The prompt names an end condition: all checks pass, or N iterations, minutes or dollars.
    • [ ] A retry cap stops the run after two failures with the same cause.
    • [ ] A cost ceiling is set, and I know where I read the real cost.
    • [ ] Results land in a file, a ticket or a PR comment, not only in the chat.
    • [ ] Running the task twice cannot send, charge or create twice.
    • [ ] A StopFailure hook records the failure and notifies me.
    • [ ] The kill switch runbook exists: disable, stop, revoke, revert.
    • [ ] The run is sandboxed, and no production keys are in its environment.

    Templates

    • Template H. Loop and schedule prompts: /loop and /schedule prompts with end condition, retry cap and "no change".
    • Template E. Long-running state files: features.json and progress.md for work that spans sessions.
    • Template B. Task contract (goal prompt): its BUDGET and STOP AND ASK ME IF lines.
    • Template F. Stop hook that blocks "done" while tests fail: counts attempts per session and logs the give-up.

    Watch out for

    • An uncapped loop. One plugin loop set to max_iterations: 0 ran 6,239 iterations over about 11.7 hours (P). Always set an iteration cap.
    • Runs that die quietly. API errors and rate limits fire StopFailure instead of Stop, so the Stop gate never runs (P).
    • No cloud dollar cap. No per-session dollar cap for cloud sessions was found, and /usage is a local estimate (P).
    • Files that vanish. A cloud run's files do not reach the next run unless merged (P).
    • A paused run that looks idle. Cloud scheduled tasks can stop and wait for an answer (P).
    • One good run. At 75% per-run success, three runs in a row all succeed only about 42% of the time, so measure pass^k (P).

    Guardrails

    Source: wiki/guardrails.md

    Use this page when you set permissions, a sandbox or an allowlist, or let an agent read untrusted input.

    Steps

    1. Start from the premise. Prompt-level guardrails are not reliable, so put controls at the tool, OS and identity boundary (D, built on P and R sources). Enforce with code and request with words. §10
    2. Prevent: write deny rules for secrets and state files. Rules evaluate deny, then ask, then allow; the first match wins, and an allow cannot carve an exception out of a deny (P). Deny rules hold in every permission mode (P).
    3. Prevent: turn the sandbox on and learn its limits. It covers Bash and its child processes only, so Read, Edit, WebFetch, MCP servers and hooks run outside it (P). Set denyRead on ~/.ssh and ~/.aws, add Read deny rules for the same paths, and set allowUnsandboxedCommands: false, because Claude can retry a failed command outside the sandbox and a matching allow rule approves that retry silently (P).
    4. Prevent: put the rules in managed settings. Managed settings sit above user, project and local settings, and allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly ignores allow, ask and deny rules from those levels, so your deny rules must live in the managed file too (P). Without a managed policy, run agents only in checkouts you trust (P).
    5. Prevent: do not treat auto mode as a boundary. An independent stress test measured 81% end-to-end false negatives across 253 actions in deliberately ambiguous scenarios, against the 17% Anthropic reports on production traffic (R). Entering auto mode drops blanket allows such as Bash(*) (P), so remove them on purpose before you rely on it (D).
    6. Prevent: cut one trifecta leg per session. An agent with private data, exposure to untrusted content and a channel to send data out can be steered into exfiltration by injected text (P). For example, run with no outbound network while it reads untrusted issues, web pages or new skills (D).
    7. Prevent: lock down headless runs and the code host. claude -p without --bare runs the repo's hooks and .mcp.json servers with no workspace trust prompt (P). Use --bare or a trusted checkout in CI, run the gate as a CI step (D), and treat issue bodies, PR comments and commit messages as untrusted input (P).
    8. Prevent: vet skills, plugins and MCP servers. A scan of 98,380 community skills confirmed 157 malicious ones, and poisoned MCP tool descriptions reached up to 72.8% attack success across 45 live servers (R). Pin versions, read the code, and treat tool descriptions as untrusted input until reviewed (D).
    9. Detect: log and alert. Append every tool call to a log with a PreToolUse hook, and alert on denials, repeated blocks and in-project writes to settings, CLAUDE.md, hooks, skills and agent definitions (D). Write logs where the agent cannot edit them, and redact secrets (D).
    10. Recover: make every run revertible. Commit or use a worktree before long runs, and snapshot memory and rule files (D). Require human approval, bound to the exact action and shown as a dry-run diff, for delete, send, publish, deploy and pay (D). §10.2

    Checklist

    • [ ] Deny rules cover secrets and state files and live in the managed file.
    • [ ] The sandbox is on, denyRead covers ~/.ssh and ~/.aws, and allowUnsandboxedCommands is false.
    • [ ] Read deny rules cover the same paths, since the sandbox does not cover the Read tool.
    • [ ] No blanket allows such as Bash(*) remain before I use auto mode.
    • [ ] Each session drops at least one leg of the lethal trifecta.
    • [ ] Skills, plugins and MCP servers are pinned and read before install.
    • [ ] CI runs claude -p with --bare or in a trusted checkout, with the gate as its own step.
    • [ ] Logs, snapshots and approval gates exist for the detect and recover layers.

    Templates

    • Template A. CLAUDE.md skeleton: its Never list is advisory, so back each line with a rule or hook.
    • Template G. PostToolUse formatter: a hook that runs outside the sandbox, so it uses the project's own Prettier, never npx.
    • Template M. PR review workflow with the Claude Code GitHub Action: scrubbed environment, minimal --allowedTools, no approval.

    Watch out for

    These are the playbook's top mistakes (§10.3).

    • Auto mode as a security boundary. Also a "95% detection" filter. Treat auto mode as convenience.
    • Bypassing permission checks with credentials mounted in the container. Dev containers do not stop credential theft in that case (P).
    • Blanket shell or interpreter allows. Remove them before you use auto mode.
    • Assuming the sandbox covers Read, hooks or MCP servers. It does not (P).
    • A cloned repo's settings with no managed policy. The repo can grant itself permissions.
    • Unreviewed skills and MCP servers. They run with your full user privileges.

    Build a harness

    Source: wiki/build-a-harness.md

    Use this page when you set up a harness around Claude for a repository, or need to decide which stage to build next.

    Steps

    1. Find your level. The roadmap runs from Level 0 (Chat) through 1 (Grounded agent), 2 (Gated), 3 (Orchestrated) and 4 (Continuous) to 5 (Self-improving). Each level has a "move up when" condition, so add the next level only when that condition holds (D). §17
    2. Level 1: write CLAUDE.md from Template A. It holds build, test and lint commands, conventions that differ from defaults, known gotchas, "never" rules and pointers to deeper docs. It leaves out what the model does anyway, long documents, secrets and stale history, and it stays short and in git (D). Cut generated /init output to what the agent can't discover (D). §8
    3. Level 1: let the agent run its own tests. Add Plan mode, the test command in CLAUDE.md and allowlisted permissions, and review plans before code (D). Write each plan as a plan file with a test per slice (Template D).
    4. Level 2: add the gates. A Stop hook, a formatter hook, receipts and your first skills, until "done" always arrives with proof (D). The runbook is verify.
    5. Level 3: add helpers. Add scout and reviewer subagents, a critic before build, worktrees for parallel builders and file-based handoffs, until you run three or more tasks in parallel without collisions (D). The runbook is orchestrate.
    6. Level 4: put state on disk. Add state files (Template E), loops, schedules, budgets, stop conditions and sandboxed unattended runs (D). The runbook is run-unattended. Level 5 is improve.
    7. Use Linear as the planning layer. The tracker holds intent and status. Issues go to humans and are delegated to agents, and the human stays the owner (P). Put repo, branch and gate rules in agent guidance once, and enforce the real gates in GitHub because guidance is advisory (P). §12.1
    8. Link PRs to issues and give each status one owner. Put the issue ID in the branch name and "Fixes ID" in the PR body, and prefer PR-based links over commit magic words (P). The agent moves an issue to In Progress, your team's GitHub automation moves it to In Review, and the merge of a PR that says "Fixes ID" moves it to Done (D).
    9. Use GitHub as the gate. Use rulesets with required checks, require code-owner review (CODEOWNERS is read from the base branch), and make CI trigger on merge_group if you use a merge queue (P). Set GITHUB_TOKEN read-only by default and grant write per job (P). §12.2
    10. Protect the self-certifying files, then add the PR review (Template M). Gate config, CI workflows, hook scripts, .claude/, CODEOWNERS and rulesets decide which checks run, so put them behind path rules and code-owner review (D). The review workflow posts findings as a comment and never approves.

    Checklist

    • [ ] I know my level (0 to 5) and the condition for moving up.
    • [ ] CLAUDE.md is short, in git, and holds commands, conventions, never rules and pointers.
    • [ ] The agent can run the test command itself.
    • [ ] Linear holds intent and status, and GitHub holds the code and the gates.
    • [ ] Branch names carry the issue ID, PRs say "Fixes ID", and each status move has an owner.
    • [ ] Gate files (gate config, workflows, hook scripts, .claude/, CODEOWNERS, rulesets) sit behind path rules and code-owner review.
    • [ ] Workflow permissions: are read-only by default, and third-party actions are pinned to full commit SHAs.
    • [ ] The advisory review workflow posts comments and never approves.

    Templates

    • Template A. CLAUDE.md skeleton: commands, conventions, never rules, when unsure, pointers.
    • Template D. Plan file: slices with a test and a rollback each.
    • Template E. Long-running state files: features.json and progress.md.
    • Template M. PR review workflow with the Claude Code GitHub Action: replace each <full-commit-sha> before use.

    Watch out for

    • Building a framework before trying one good call. Try one well-built call with good context first (§15, P).
    • A giant CLAUDE.md. Claude Code's best practices warn that a bloated file gets ignored (P). Keep detailed learnings in docs/solutions/ or skills.
    • Must-happen checks that live only in prose. Put them in hooks, CI, permissions or the sandbox.
    • An agent that edits its own gates. Any change to the self-certifying files is high risk (D).
    • Commit magic words. They can close a Linear issue as soon as a commit lands on the default branch, skipping review (P).
    • pull_request_target. It runs base-branch code with secrets, so running PR code there is a "pwn request" (P). Do not switch to it to fix fork PRs in Template M.

    Where records live

    Source: wiki/records.md

    Use this page when agent work produces decisions, plans or state that must outlive one chat: a grill, a plan, a long run, delegated helpers, a ticket.

    Why not the chat

    • Recall degrades as the context window fills, so treat it as a budget (P). Law 4
    • Models forget between sessions; the countermeasure is CLAUDE.md, memory and progress files (P). §14
    • Long runs keep progress and decision files outside the window (P). §8
    • Helpers write outputs to files and pass back references, never raw transcripts (P). §7

    Steps

    1. Sort each record by lifetime (D), using the table below.
    2. Write decisions in the repo, not only in chat: question or decision, answer, reason, date (D). §5.2
    3. Keep task state in files: JSON for status the agent must not casually rewrite, Markdown for notes, git as the audit trail (P). §8, §11.1
    4. Track the work item in the tracker and link both ways: the issue links the plan file, and the plan names the issue id (D). PRs link the issue by id in the title, with "Fixes ID" in the body (P). §12.1
    5. Push decisions with the branch, so reviewers, CI and other sessions see them and they merge with the code (D).
    6. Close out: when the task merges, fold lasting decisions into docs/decisions.md or the plan, and delete progress files and scratch (D).
    RecordWhereCommit and push?
    Grill decisionsdocs/discovery/<topic>.mdYes
    Plan and its decisionsdocs/plans/<task>.md (Template D)Yes
    Routing and other lasting decisionsdocs/decisions.md, one dated line eachYes
    Long-run statefeatures.json, progress.md (Template E)Yes while the run lasts; delete or fold in at the end
    Work item, status, blockersThe tracker issue (Template L), short commentsLives in the tracker
    Final receiptThe PR description, one line in the issueWith the PR
    Prompts that /prompt generatesThe guide's prompts/<project>/, git-ignored (prompts/README.md)No: kept on your machine only
    Helper output, transcripts, dumpsAn ignored folder (for example .agent/) or the session scratchpadNo

    Recommended flow

    1. /grill <idea> logs each decision to docs/discovery/<topic>.md.
    2. Write the issue with Template L and link the discovery file.
    3. Branch <issue-id>-<slug>; /guide logs the chosen route to docs/decisions.md; the plan in docs/plans/<task>.md names the issue id.
    4. Helpers write findings to scratch files and return a summary with paths.
    5. Open the PR with the issue id in its title, "Fixes ID" and the receipt in its body.
    6. Merge; the issue closes, and the decisions land on main with the code.

    Checklist

    • [ ] No decision exists only in chat.
    • [ ] Each decision line has a date and a reason.
    • [ ] The issue links the plan, and the plan names the issue id.
    • [ ] Scratch output is ignored by git.
    • [ ] Progress files were deleted or folded in when the task closed.

    Templates

    • Template D. Plan file: the Decisions list.
    • Template E. Long-running state files: features.json and progress.md.
    • Template L. Agent-ready issue: the tracker item.

    Watch out for

    • Two copies of one log. A ticket and a file drift apart; link, don't copy.
    • One log file per session. Use one file per topic or task.
    • A temporary worktree as storage. Uncommitted files go when it is cleaned up; commit decisions on the branch.
    • A repo you don't own. Keep logs in your own notes, and post only the decisions into the PR or ticket.
    • Linear agent threads get archived (S), so durable state lives in files or labels. §12.1

    Improve

    Source: wiki/improve.md

    Use this page after real tasks, when you want the harness to get better, or when the model keeps repeating a bad habit.

    Steps

    1. Hold a retro after each real task (Template I). Ask where turns were wasted, what you had to correct, which check caught a real problem, which check was missing and which helper came back empty. Propose up to 3 changes, and apply none until you say yes (D).
    2. Turn each lesson into one change. A change is a CLAUDE.md rule, a skill, a hook, a test or a tool fix (D). Keep detailed learnings in docs/solutions/ or skills, and promote to CLAUDE.md only the rules that stop a repeated mistake (D). Keep a mined rule or skill only if re-running the evals shows it helps (D). §13 Law 8
    3. Start an eval set from real failures. Collect 20 to 50 simple tasks drawn from real failures (P), one JSONL line per task (Template J). Record where each task came from, such as an incident (D).
    4. Pick graders and read transcripts. Code-based graders are fast, objective and brittle, model-based graders need calibration, and humans are the gold standard but slow (P). Prefer code checks before LLM judges, and validate any judge against expert labels (P). Scores say that something broke; transcripts say why (P). Label failures by hand (D). §13
    5. Track the scorecard. Count first-try pass rate, rework loops, human interventions, escaped defects, cost per task and pass^k on the eval set (D). Read the trend after ten tasks to see where to invest, as page Lesson 13 (Growing) advises.
    6. Change one thing at a time. Keep CLAUDE.md, agent definitions, skills, hooks and tool descriptions in git, and re-run the eval set after each change (D). On a model upgrade, re-run with components removed and delete what no longer earns its tokens (D).
    7. Prune on a schedule. Cut any line whose removal would not cause a mistake (P), and drop rules that never fire (D).
    8. Match the symptom to its countermeasure. Look the bad habit up in the failure-mode table and apply its fix. When the same check fails twice for the same reason, stop and ask for a second opinion (D). §14
    9. Audit the design against the anti-patterns. Examples are a framework built before one good call, the builder grading its own work, and loops with no cap (P, D). §15
    10. Watch the review load. Cap PR size, route review depth by risk tier, and track approval rate and time-to-review (D). A near-100% approval rate with falling review time is the warning sign of normalization of deviance (D).

    Checklist

    • [ ] A retro ran after my last real task, and each proposal was accepted or rejected.
    • [ ] Each accepted lesson became a rule, skill, hook, test or tool fix.
    • [ ] The eval set holds tasks from real failures, one JSONL line each.
    • [ ] I read transcripts of failing runs, not only scores.
    • [ ] The scorecard tracks six measures, and I looked at the trend after ten tasks.
    • [ ] After a model upgrade I re-ran a frozen eval set with k trials per task.
    • [ ] I pruned CLAUDE.md lines and rules that never fire.
    • [ ] I looked at approval rate and time-to-review.

    Templates

    • Template I. Retro prompt: up to 3 changes with exact text, applied only after you say yes.
    • Template J. Eval task record (JSONL, one line per task): id, source, prompt, grader, check, expected, tags and trials.
    • Template A. CLAUDE.md skeleton: where promoted rules land.

    Watch out for

    • Declares victory early (P). Counter with a JSON feature list, end-to-end tests and a Stop hook.
    • Edits, disables or deletes tests to make them pass (P). Add a test-immutability rule plus a hook or CODEOWNERS on test paths.
    • Loops on the same failing approach (P). Add a retry cap and a second opinion from a fresh agent.
    • Sycophancy and no pushback (S). Use independent reviewers who do not see the author's reasoning, or anonymized councils.
    • Overbuilds and adds features nobody asked for (S, P). Set a diff-size budget, write no-gos into the issue, and have the reviewer flag scope creep.
    • A bloated CLAUDE.md (P). It gets ignored, so prune it and move detail into skills or docs/solutions/.

    Go deeper

    • §13 Evals and learning: graders, the scorecard and the learning loop.
    • §14 Model failure modes and countermeasures: the full table, including jagged competence and context rot.
    • §15 Anti-patterns
    • §18 Operating the harness: gaps to close: evals across model upgrades and human review load.
    • §19.1 Findings that hold up: finding 9, evals start from error analysis.
    • Law 1. Keep the harness thin; let the model do the work

    • Related runbooks: build-a-harness, verify.

    Unstick an agent

    Source: wiki/unstick.md

    Use this page when a Claude agent loops, will not finish, says "done" over broken work, repeats a mistake, loses context in a long session or builds more than you asked for.

    Symptoms

    SymptomLikely causeFirst movePlaybook
    Same error twice, or the same fix tried againLoops on the same failing approach (P)Stop it. Ask for 3 ranked hypotheses and one test that separates them, or bring in a fresh reviewer agent§14, cheat sheet §3
    Busy, no progressNo checkable next stepAsk "What is the next checkable step, and what proves it is done?"§4, cheat sheet §3
    "Done" with no proofDeclares victory early (P)Ask "Receipt please: PASS, FAIL or NOT RUN, with the command for each"§14, cheat sheet §3
    Tests pass, but the tests changedEdits, disables or deletes tests to make them pass (P)Read the test diff. Add a test-immutability rule plus a hook or CODEOWNERS on test paths§14
    Forgets earlier decisions in a long sessionContext rot (P)/compact <focus>, or start a new session from the plan file§14, cheat sheet §3
    Repeats an old mistake in a new sessionForgets between sessions (P)Put the lesson in CLAUDE.md, memory or a progress file§14, §8
    Builds extras, bloats, leaves dead codeOverbuilds (S); adds features nobody asked for (P)Set a diff-size budget, write no-gos into the issue, ask for a simplifier pass§14
    Waiting on permissionA permission prompt is blocking itCheck the sidebar for "waiting". Pre-allow safe commands in settingsCheat sheet §3
    Silent background agentThe helper went quietAsk for status. If nothing comes back, stop it and re-brief it with narrower scopeCheat sheet §3

    Steps

    1. Break a loop. When the same check fails twice for the same reason, stop and get a second opinion: 3 ranked hypotheses and one test that separates them, or a fresh agent (P). The loop escalates to a second opinion or a human, never a sixth retry (D). §4
    2. Restore a checkable step. If it is busy with no progress, ask what the next checkable step is and what proves it done. The loop takes one small step toward a "done when" item and verifies it before the next (D). §4
    3. Replace "done" with a receipt. Ask for PASS, FAIL or NOT RUN with the command for each item. NOT RUN is not PASS. A JSON feature list, end-to-end tests and a Stop hook counter early victory (P). Models also edit, disable or delete tests to make them pass (P), so read the test diff and guard test paths with a hook or CODEOWNERS. §14
    4. Rescue a long session. Run /compact <focus>, or start a new session from the plan file, which is the source of truth, so keep it current. Counter context rot with subagents, compaction and notes on disk (P). Keep progress and decisions in files: JSON for state such as feature lists, Markdown for narrative notes (P). §8
    5. Cut overbuilding. Set a diff-size budget, ask for a simplifier pass and have the reviewer flag scope creep (S). Write no-gos into the issue for features nobody asked for (P). §14
    6. Unblock a helper or a prompt. Check the sidebar for "waiting" and pre-allow safe commands in settings. If a background agent is silent, ask for status, then stop it and re-brief it with narrower scope. Cheat sheet §3
    7. Cap the next run. Give it a stop condition (every check passes, or N iterations, minutes or dollars), a retry cap (after two failures with the same cause, stop and report) and a results sink outside the chat (D). When the budget runs out, stop and report. The Stop-hook continuation cap of 8 is a backstop, not your stop condition (P). §11.3
    8. Hand the lesson to a retro. Run Template I and propose up to 3 changes: a CLAUDE.md rule, a skill, a hook, a test or a tool fix. Apply none until you say yes (D). Promote to CLAUDE.md only the rules that stop a repeated mistake (D). Law 8

    Checklist

    • [ ] After two failures with the same cause, a fresh agent or I gave a second opinion.
    • [ ] Every "done" has a receipt with PASS, FAIL or NOT RUN and the command, and NOT RUN is not PASS.
    • [ ] I read the test diff, and test paths are guarded by a hook or CODEOWNERS.
    • [ ] Decisions and progress live in files, so a new session can start from the plan file.
    • [ ] The goal names no-gos and a diff-size budget.
    • [ ] The next run has a stop condition, a retry cap and a results sink outside the chat.
    • [ ] I ran a retro, and each proposed change was accepted or rejected.

    Templates

    • Template B. Task contract (goal prompt): the Done-when lines, the budget, the stop-and-ask list and the RULES block.
    • Template D. Plan file: the file a fresh session starts from.
    • Template C. Subagent brief: re-brief a silent helper with a narrower scope.
    • Template F. Stop hook that blocks "done" while tests fail: enforces "done" with code, because must-happen checks that live only in prose are an anti-pattern.
    • Template I. Retro prompt: up to 3 changes, applied only after you say yes.

    Watch out for

    • Loops with no cap. They keep going (§15). Set the iteration, time or cost cap before you restart.
    • A second opinion that read the first answer. Give the fresh agent the failing check and the criteria, not the first agent's reasoning (S).
    • Trusting skill across areas. Competence is jagged, so verify everything (P). On genuinely novel code, use more human design, smaller steps and closer collaboration (P, S).

    Go deeper

    • §14 Model failure modes and countermeasures: the full table, including hidden trade-offs and sycophancy.
    • §4 The core loop (one agent): where escalation sits, and the order to verify in.
    • §8 Context engineering: compaction, notes, subagents and state formats.
    • §11.3 Guardrails for any loop: stop condition, retry cap and results sink.
    • §15 Anti-patterns
    • Cheat sheet §3. Stuck signs and fixes: six signs and one-line fixes.
    • Page lessons: page Lesson 1 (Everything is one loop), page Lesson 15 (When it goes wrong).
    • Related runbooks: verify, improve, run-unattended.

    Case study: this repository

    Source: wiki/case-study.md

    Read this page to see the playbook applied from first request to final review, on the work that built this repository's teaching page and playbook.

    Background

    On 2026-10-24, one Claude Code session in the Claude desktop app built the "Orchestrating Claude" page and the playbook (session log). The owner then asked for independent reviews, and the rest of the work ran the way the playbook says to run it. Each section below names the files that show it. The decision log records each choice as D1 to D27.

    The steps and the playbook sections they applied

    #StepRule appliedPlaybook
    1A request becomes an issue with 13 childrenSlice into issues with an outcome, a check, a boundary and dependencies; write a task contract and a plan table; scale the lifecycle to the risk§5.1, Template L, Template B, Template D, §5.4
    2The check harness comes firstNo task without a check the agent can run itself; criterion, scenario, then gateLaw 2, §9.1
    3One writer on the page, parallel draftersSingle agent for tightly coupled edits, fan out for parallel work, one writer per set of filesLaw 10, §7, §19.1
    4Reviewers who never saw the builder's reportSeparate the maker from the checker; reviewers get the artifact and the criteria onlyLaw 7, §9.2 (rung 4), §7
    5A doc-checker fact-check changes a chartSpot-check a number against its source before quoting it; a helper's report is a claim, not proof§19, §7
    6A 30-minute launch with a written cutAppetite is a time budget with variable scope; a budget and a stop-and-report rule; a minutes-based stop condition§5.1, Template B, §11.3
    7Gates, version by version, v12 to v16A receipt of PASS, FAIL or NOT RUN with the command; NOT RUN is not PASS; a test and a rollback per slice§9.4, §5.4, Template D
    8A final review catches a P1 keyboard bugTests can pass while the spec is still violated (S), so keep a fresh-eyes review; turn each lesson into a test§9.3, §13

    1. A request becomes an issue with 13 children

    • The owner asked for independent UI/UX, learning-psychology and charting reviews, then an issue for a builder (session log, step 13). The reviews hold 38 findings: UX-1 to UX-13, LX-1 to LX-11 and VZ-1 to VZ-14.
    • The issue has a parent and children 0 to 12, each a Template L issue with an outcome, a check, a boundary and a risk. A triage map sends every finding to a child, reviewer conflicts (C1 to C4) are settled in writing, and four open questions (Q1 to Q4) carry a recommended default.
    • Severity runs from P0 (child 7) to P3 (child 12). The review tier is T1, so the gate is the check script plus a fresh re-review.
    • The issue ends with a Template D plan table and a Template B contract: six Done-when lines, at most 3 helpers at a time, and a stop after 2 failed attempts at one check or 13 publishes without a new PASS.

    2. The check harness comes first

    • Child 0 built checks/static.sh, checks/dom-checks.js and checks/run-dom.js before any page edit (checks README).
    • It ran them on version 11 and saved the baseline: 12 PASS, 57 FAIL. The failures included page overflow at 320 and 375 px, 155 SVG labels under 12px on phones, an evidence chart whose caption named 4 benchmarks while it drew 3, and an arrow key that moved focus to the wrong node.
    • The run also settled a doubt: the UX review could not verify the desktop h1 overflow, and the baseline showed it was real.
    • Template B's first two Done-when lines require the checks to print only PASS.

    3. One writer on the page, parallel drafters

    • Every page child edits one HTML file, so the plan runs them one at a time: one writer (plan order note). Decision D19 let subagents work in parallel on other files, on drafts and on reviews, with the lead splicing the output.
    • The playbook navigation (child 5) ran in its own file at the same time. The glossary, takeaways and running example were drafted in issues/drafts. Two figure agents redrew four diagrams, and tools/splice_figs.py spliced them in. The contract capped helpers at 3.

    4. Reviewers who never saw the builder's report

    • Decision D20: reviewers are fresh agents that get the files and the brief, never the builder's report. The session log lists them as fresh Sonnet subagents.
    • The playbook-navigation reviewer ran its own scripts and was not shown the builder's report. It passed the change, and its low-severity notes went into a follow-up (review).
    • The plan table marked child 7 (honest charts) PASS on the builder's own checks while the chart review was still running. The independent chart reviewer then returned FAIL with three blocking items, all fixed in version 15 (review).
    • A fresh reviewer re-ran the three original briefs on version 12 and found 14 fixed, 22 partly fixed and 2 open (review).
    • The reason appears in page Lesson 6 (Orchestration): a reviewer that reads your conclusion tends to agree with it.

    5. A doc-checker fact-check changes a chart

    • The chart in page Lesson 17 (Evidence) plots the Google Research scaling study. doc-checker checked its claims against the arXiv text for versions 1 and 3 and the Google Research blog (fact-check).
    • It found that the page's counts (180 configurations, 4 benchmarks) match version 1, while version 3 reports 260 configurations and 6 benchmarks. It found that the 45% threshold is a fitted crossover, not an observed cliff, and that 17.2× and 4.4× are relative to a single agent.
    • D11 replaced the bar chart with a dot plot: all four benchmarks, the best and worst design, exact baselines, a data table and the words "read the direction, not the size". D12 cites paper version 1 (December 2025) and hedges the threshold. The chart reviewer later confirmed the numbers match the fact-check, and the playbook took the same correction in version 0.4.
    • Template B made this a Done-when line: doc-checker confirms every number in the chart and its table.

    6. A 30-minute launch with a written cut

    • The owner set a 30-minute limit for a production launch (session log, step 16).
    • Decision D21 wrote the cut down: ship children 0 to 7, 9, 10 and the takeaways; defer child 8, the rest of child 11, and child 12. The owner set the limit and Claude chose the cut.
    • The cut kept the P0 child and every P1 child (1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 10) and deferred only P2 and P3 work. Version 12 went out with 20 of 20 checks passing in 6 views, and the deferred children shipped in version 15.

    7. Gates, version by version, v12 to v16

    VersionChangeGate result
    12The 30-minute launch20 of 20 in 6 views
    13Phase buttons under the diagram, panel height heldSteady over 18 clicks in 3 views
    14Phase nav centered, "← Prev" and "Next →"Steady and symmetric at 1280, 375 and 320 px
    15Review fixes, child 8, the rest of child 11, child 1220 of 20 in 6 views
    16Final review fixes21 of 21 in 8 views
    • Source: version history. Each version went to the same URL after its own check passed (D27), and new checks were added with each child (D26).
    • The plan table holds a rollback for every slice: "republish previous version". Receipts say what did not run: the test-reader check is "not run" for children 2 and 3, and the scripted term count for child 11.

    8. A final review catches a P1 keyboard bug

    • Version 15 passed 20 of 20 checks. A fresh read-only reviewer then checked the page source against all 38 original findings and returned "not ready" (final review).
    • The P1: the quiz's change listener locked a question on the first arrow key, so a keyboard user could not choose an answer. Decision D23 fixed it with a "Check answer" button for each question.
    • Version 16 added the check quiz-1, which asserts that arrows only select and Check answer scores, and ran the checks in 8 views instead of 6. The reviewer also found a P2 (figure text under 12px between 721 and 1230 px) and five P3 items, all fixed in version 16.
    • Its tally on the 38 original findings was 27 fixed, 11 partly fixed and 0 open.

    What stayed open

    • Vertical phone variants for figures were deferred, so UX-3 and VZ-3 are only partly fixed.
    • The blind test-reader check was not run. The reviewer's 5 of 5 on the quiz does not count, because it saw the answers in the source first.
    • Two reviewer proposals were declined: reordering the lessons (D4, question Q1) and tap-to-preview on touch screens (D2, question Q2).

    Go deeper

    • Repository records: session log, decision log, version history, the issue.
    • §0 How to use this file: what the grade (S) means.
    • Page lessons: page Lesson 3 (Idea to issues), page Lesson 6 (Orchestration), page Lesson 9 (Self-checks), page Lesson 17 (Evidence).
    • Runbooks for each step: start-a-task, orchestrate, verify, improve.

    Claude Code cheat sheet

    Source: playbook/claude-cheat-sheet.md

    Companion to agent-harness-playbook.md. Command names change between releases; type / or /help to see what your version supports.

    1. Which surface

    SurfaceUse it forGives up
    Terminal (claude)Newest features first, scripting (claude -p), worktrees (claude -w), --cloud, teleport, Remote ControlDiff pane, browser, visuals
    Desktop, Code tabControl room: many sessions side by side, built-in browser, artifacts, task lists, splitting work into new sessions, phone follow-alongSome CLI-only commands (/permissions, /config)
    VS Code extensionReading and reviewing diffs inline, shared file and selection context, small edits while you codeRunning many sessions in parallel
    claude.ai/code and phoneUnattended cloud runs, steering from anywhereLocal files, unless you use Remote Control

    Default: Desktop as the control room, Terminal for scripts and CLI-only features, VS Code when reading code line by line. All of them share ~/.claude (CLAUDE.md, skills, hooks, agents), so switching costs nothing.

    2. Commands

    NeedCommand
    Side question without derailing/btw <question>
    What fills the context/context
    Shrink context, keep a focus/compact <focus>
    Start clean/clear
    Cost/usage
    Plan before buildingShift+Tab to plan mode
    InterruptEsc
    Go back to an earlier turnEsc Esc, or /rewind
    Continue or pick a sessionclaude -c, /resume
    See running sessionsclaude agents, Desktop sidebar, or ask "list current sessions and their status"
    Manage subagents/agents
    Repeat a prompt in this session/loop
    Cloud runs on a timetable/schedule
    Keep going until a condition holds/goal <condition>
    Split mechanical changes into many PRs/batch

    3. Stuck signs and fixes

    SignFix
    Same error twiceStop it. Ask for 3 ranked hypotheses and one test that separates them, or bring in a fresh reviewer agent
    Busy, no progress"What is the next checkable step, and what proves it is done?"
    Forgets earlier decisions/compact <focus>, or a new session started from the plan file
    Waiting on permissionCheck the sidebar for "waiting"; pre-allow safe commands in settings
    Silent background agentAsk for status; if nothing comes back, stop it and re-brief it with narrower scope
    "Done" with no proof"Receipt please: PASS, FAIL or NOT RUN, with the command for each"

    4. Mindset

    • Give outcomes and how you will check them, not step-by-step instructions.
    • Plan first; get a fresh critic for anything risky.
    • One agent writes; helpers only read and review.
    • Turn each repeated correction into a rule ("update CLAUDE.md so this does not repeat"); prune rules that never fire.
    • Put "stop and ask me if..." lines and a budget in every long task.
    • Be specific: file paths, examples, constraints.

    5. Voice input (Wispr Flow)

    • Dictation suits agents: longer, richer prompts beat terse ones.
    • Read file names, commands and flags back before sending; dictation mangles them.
    • Do not let cleanup soften constraints. "Do not touch X" must survive word for word.

    6. Prompt template for orchestrated work

    Goal: <outcome, one sentence>
Context: <files, links, prior decisions>
Done when: <checkable test, command, or acceptance list>
Constraints: <must not touch, budget, style>
Stop and ask if: <risky or ambiguous cases>
Plan: interview me first, then write a plan file before building.
Orchestration: one writer; read-only subagents for search and review.
Report: receipt per change (PASS/FAIL/NOT RUN with the command).

    7. Let Claude draft the prompt

    1. Brain-dump the idea (voice works well).
    2. "Interview me one question at a time until you can write the brief."
    3. "Write the brief using the template above, into a file."
    4. Edit the goal, done-when and stop-and-ask lines yourself. Those carry your judgment.
    5. Start a fresh session from the file.

    Tools and agents used

    • Browsers: the built-in browser pane, for checking the published page while signed in; Playwright (Chromium), for the automated checks on a local wrapped copy.
    • Research: Firecrawl, Exa and web search through research subagents. doc-checker handled primary-source fact checks.
    • Reviewers: fresh Sonnet subagents, given files and briefs and never the builder's conclusions.
    • Builders in parallel: a Sonnet subagent for the playbook (child 5); drafting agents for the glossary, takeaways and running example; two figure agents that wrote SVG drafts for the lead to splice in.
    • Palette check: the dataviz skill's validate_palette.js, which ruled out green against red on the evidence chart.
